executive_summary: August 2026 presents a striking paradox: investors are increasingly eager to buy the dip and broadly expect stocks to rise over the next year, yet crash anxiety has actually intensified. Meanwhile, institutional investors have grown notably more comfortable with valuations, though individuals remain skeptical. The overall picture is one of cautious optimism laced with nervous energy — investors who like the market's direction but aren't entirely sure the road will be smooth.

key_findings.headline: Institutions Bounce Back Strongly
key_findings.interpretation: Institutional confidence in a market rise over the next 12 months rebounded sharply to 85.71% after dipping to 66.67% in July, while individual confidence slipped back to 72.22% from 80.0%. This divergence may reflect different reactions to the same news — or simply that professional money managers and individual investors are weighting different signals.

key_findings.headline: Crash Fears Quietly Intensify
key_findings.interpretation: Only 30% of institutional investors and 22% of individuals feel confident a crash won't happen in the next six months — both readings down from July. In plain terms, the vast majority of both groups see a meaningful crash as at least plausible, even as they remain broadly optimistic about the year ahead.

key_findings.headline: Dip-Buying Faith Surges Dramatically
key_findings.interpretation: Every single institutional respondent and nearly nine in ten individuals now believe a 3% daily drop would fully recover within two days — an enormous jump from July's readings near 45% for both groups. This could reflect recent experience with quick recoveries, or a broader belief that eager buyers are waiting on the sidelines to snap up any discount.

key_findings.headline: Valuation Views Diverge Sharply
key_findings.interpretation: Two-thirds of institutional investors now say the market is not overvalued, up from 60% in July, while individuals held steady at 40%. It's worth noting that some institutional investors subscribe to market-efficiency frameworks where the current price is, by definition, the right price — making the overvaluation question something of a non-starter for them.

detailed_analysis:
The headline story of August is a remarkable surge in dip-buying conviction. Institutional buy-on-dips confidence jumped from 45.45% to a perfect 100%, and individuals followed suit, climbing from 45.45% to 87.5%. Think of it like a crowded theater where everyone suddenly believes the exits are wide enough — reassuring in calm times, but potentially dangerous if the crowd ever tests that assumption at once. Whether this reflects genuine market resilience or a complacency built on recent good fortune is an open question.

At the same time, crash confidence moved in the opposite direction. Only 30% of institutions and 22% of individuals are confident a crash won't materialize in the next six months, down from 50% and 27% respectively in July. This creates an unusual psychological profile: most investors simultaneously believe the market will bounce back quickly from any stumble, yet also acknowledge that a serious crash is a real possibility. One reading of this is that investors have mentally separated short-term volatility from catastrophic risk — they trust the recovery mechanism but not the road itself.

Institutional one-year confidence snapped back to 85.71% after a soft July, suggesting last month's dip in optimism may have been a temporary wobble rather than a trend change. Individual one-year confidence, by contrast, edged lower. This kind of institutional-individual gap isn't unusual — professional managers often react more quickly to shifting macro data, while individuals may be more influenced by headlines and personal portfolio experience.

On valuations, the institutional-individual split is now the widest it's been in the three-month window. Roughly two-thirds of institutions see prices as fair or cheap, compared to just four in ten individuals. Some of this gap may stem from philosophical differences: market-efficiency adherents in the institutional camp may regard the overvaluation question as essentially moot. For those who do engage with it, the disagreement could reflect different assumptions about earnings growth, interest rates, or simply different gut feelings about whether stocks have gotten ahead of themselves.
methodology: These indices come from the Yale/Shiller U.S. Stock Market Confidence Surveys, which have tracked investor sentiment since 1989. Each month, roughly 100 wealthy individual investors and 100 institutional investment managers answer the same standardized questions. The consistency of those questions over 35+ years is what makes the data meaningful — you can actually compare investor psychology across very different market environments. The four indices each measure something distinct: • 1-Year Confidence: The share who expect prices to be higher in 12 months. • Crash Confidence: The share who believe a crash in the next 6 months is very unlikely (under 10% probability). A low reading means most people think a crash is plausible. • Buy-on-Dips Confidence: The share who believe that after a 3% single-day market drop, prices would fully recover within two days. • Valuation Confidence: The share who do not believe the market is overvalued. Surveys were conducted semi-annually before 2001 and have been monthly since July 2001. Respondents rotate over time, but consistent characteristics — high income, investment experience — are maintained across the panel.
